strongest_case_for:
1. The format rewards one hard-to-fake measurement, and Case 3 already has it. Round 1 is one PDF slide read by assessors and a jury shortlisting from (Season 2 precedent) thousands of teams [verified_fact for format; unverified_assumption for scale]. On this very laptop, a 70-line shell script (evidence/wsl2_tc_testbed_check.sh, run by the technical skeptic on 2026-10-18) produced: mean RTT under a bulk download 638.0 ms -> 41.2 ms (max 3534 -> 42.4 ms), WAN backlog 674 -> 17 packets, bulk throughput 15.9 -> 16.4 Mbps, i.e. a 93.5% latency cut with zero throughput loss, on the first run [verified_fact, single run, WSL2 emulation]. Case 1's headline is RMSE 14.2 on a benchmark with 53 public repos: correct, reproducible, and indistinguishable from every other competent entry [verified_fact for the count; technical_inference for indistinguishability]. The prior report itself lists "judges reward visible, dramatic, hard-to-fake measurements" as a condition that flips the decision to Case 3.

2. The PDF prescribes the Round-2 evidence format, and it is exactly "prototype as annex". Case 3's Expected Output demands "Automated baseline-versus-optimized experiments" and an "Automated or scripted demonstration that can reset the environment, introduce the selected condition, collect evidence and generate a result report" [source_derived_requirement]. A report.html with tables, a repo with `make demo`, and a short recording IS the deliverable; no live demo is required to earn the marks. The red-team flagged that Case 1's "Working pipeline 20% + Demo & explanation 20%" is harder to evidence through a deck [technical_inference].

3. All five criteria are measurable with ground truth the testbed controls (true capacity = the netem/HTB rate the script set), so every criterion maps to a numbered table with confidence intervals; four of the five are earned by enforcement plus the experiment pipeline, which is Python/JSON/CLI/CI work. AI is optional ("Where AI is used") and penalised if it only adds a chat interface, so the team is not forced into ML research [source_derived_requirement].

4. The system-level niche is empty while Case 1's is the most crowded. No repo on the GitHub 'qos' (278) or 'traffic-shaping' (94) topic pages is an intent-aware, self-verifying home controller with confidence, rollback and a dashboard; cake-autorate, sqm-autorate, PURPLE, qosify, LibreQoS, FlowQoS and the closed-loop IBN paper all lack verify-then-rollback [verified_fact for the search]. The "hypothesis-verify-rollback" actuator maps one-to-one onto four PDF constraints (verify improvement, policy rollback, bounded/observable/reversible remediation, return to a known safe state) and addresses a failure mode the incumbents document themselves (sqm-autorate README: unrelated latency spikes drive rate to minimum) [verified_fact]. Case 1, as the only case with a provided dataset and explicit weights, plausibly attracts the largest and most ML-capable pool [HYP].

5. The skill-fit penalty (6.0, the number that decided the ranking) is overstated for this team with Claude Max. The differentiating modules (action ledger, verify window, FastAPI /intent and /correct, invariants, experiment runner with bootstrap CIs, report generator, React dashboard, GitHub Actions) are backend engineering. The kernel-adjacent surface is iproute2 commands that are fully documented in man pages, already proven on this machine, and were written and debugged by an AI agent in one session. The skeptic's own words: "my own one-script testbed produced a 93% latency reduction on the first run, so the floor is higher than the specialist's skill_fit=6 implies" [verified_fact for the quote; technical_inference for the conclusion].

6. The finale audience is senior Tata Elxsi leaders and the case is tagged MCV (media and communications), their own vertical [verified_fact for the tag; technical_inference for judge composition]. "Your work call stays smooth while someone downloads an ISO, and the controller undoes any change that did not help" is understood by every executive in one sentence; Case 1's differentiator (conformal lower-bound triage with a leakage-free decision-replay harness) needs three.

7. The prior report's own sensitivity analysis says the decision is a toss-up (8.23 vs 8.13 on base weights; all three adversarial reviewers say Case 1 loses) once Linux networking fluency is present. Seven weeks, AI assistance throughout, and a working testbed script are a credible substitute for that fluency, and the Week-1 gate below makes the bet reversible before anything is submitted.
round1_single_slide_plan:
WHAT THE SLIDE MUST SHOW (assessors skim; the slide is scored on whether it is credible, specific and different in ten seconds):
- Header (one line): "Verify-or-Rollback QoS: an intent-aware home-gateway controller that proves every policy change helped, on open Linux tc" plus the PDF's own scenario in the subtitle ("ISO download during a video call").
- Block A, the evidence box (top-right, largest element): one bar/strip chart, baseline vs controlled, mean and max RTT under load (638 -> 41 ms; 3534 -> 42 ms), backlog (674 -> 17 pkts) and bulk throughput (15.9 -> 16.4 Mbps), captioned exactly: "Linux network-namespace emulation on WSL2, netem 20 Mbps / 20 ms, HTB + fq_codel, 2026-10-18, script in repo". Label as emulation and as a preliminary run; by submission day replace with the N=5 or N=10 median and 95% CI (see schedule). This is the element no design-only slide can match.
- Block B, architecture strip (device -> edge -> network -> data -> analytics -> UI, the six components the PDF names): LAN devices -> router namespace [classifier (broad categories, confidence, /correct) -> capacity estimator (latency feedback, scored against ground truth) -> policy engine (HTB floors >= 5%, sum <= 90%, fq_codel leaves) -> enforce (tc flower, IPv4/IPv6)] -> WAN; side loop: verify window -> keep or rollback -> action ledger; watchdog -> safe state (fq_codel only); intent API with TTL; dashboard.
- Block C, "what is new vs OpenWrt SQM / cake-autorate" (three bullets, naming the prior art honestly): every shaping action is a logged hypothesis with a predicted KPI, a bounded verification window and automatic revert with backoff; estimator error and convergence time published against controlled ground truth; one-command, seeded, CI-reproduced experiment suite with confidence intervals.
- Block D, criteria-to-evidence table (5 rows, one line each): classification/link accuracy -> confusion matrix + estimator error %; latency/jitter/loss -> irtt p95/IPDV/loss baseline vs optimised; fairness -> Jain index + bulk floor never breached; adaptation/stability -> time-to-recover after 100->20 Mbps, rate flips/min, three-arm ablation (no controller / open-loop AIMD / verify-or-rollback); CPU/reproducibility -> controller CPU%, `make demo`, CI run.
- Block E, boundary and roadmap (two lines): emulation, no decryption, licences documented; production would use CAKE/connmark/IFB/offload; Round-2 milestones.

CAN IT BE PRODUCED CONVINCINGLY IN SIX DAYS: yes, with one gate. Day 1 (19 Oct): every teammate runs the existing check script under `wsl -u root`; apt-install iperf3 and irtt (irtt is packaged in Ubuntu noble [verified_fact]). Day 2 (20 Oct): extend the script into `make demo SCENARIO=1 RUNS=5` with per-ping RTT capture, p95, median-of-runs and a JSON/PNG output (AI-assisted, mostly Python). GATE at end of Day 2: if the 5-run report reproduces the >= 80% p95 reduction on at least one teammate's machine, commit to Case 3; if the environment fails on all machines, submit Case 1 instead (its Round-1 content is already drafted in the prior report). Days 3-4: diagram and slide (HTML or PowerPoint exported to PDF; keep well under 5 MB, the Season 3 precedent [unverified_assumption]); Day 5: check every PDF constraint bullet is visibly addressed and the prior-art names are present; Day 6 (24 Oct): submit before midday IST, not at 23:59. Risk accepted: the skeptic noted the specialist never planned a Round-1 artefact and that compressing nine expected outputs into one slide is harder than Case 1's prescribed deck items [source_derived_requirement]; the mitigation is that the evidence box carries the slide and the architecture strip is the PDF's own six-component list.
round2_plan_8_weeks:
Calendar: 25 Oct to 13 Dec is seven weeks (eight from today); the shortlist date is unknown (somewhere between 24 Oct and 14 Nov), so Weeks 1-3 are spent at risk of not being shortlisted, identically for Case 1. Assume 2-3 students at ~12-15 h/week each plus AI assistance, i.e. roughly 250-300 h; the prior skeptic warns effort estimates run ~40% light, so the plan below puts the differentiator in the middle, not at the end, and keeps dashboard, ML, IPv6 and CAKE off the critical path [technical_inference].

Week 1 (25-31 Oct) Testbed and evidence pipeline. `make doctor` (WSL >= 2.3.11, modprobe -n for sch_htb/sch_netem/sch_fq_codel/cls_flower/ifb, iperf3/irtt present, root); six LAN namespaces (call, game, tv1-3, bulk) + router + WAN; traffic generators with JSON output (irtt 20 ms/172 B call probe, UDP game stream, three CBR TV streams, iperf3 bulk); collector sampling `tc -j -s` at 1 Hz plus psutil; report generator with medians and bootstrap 95% CIs. Exit: Scenario 1 at N=10 produces report.md (table E2). Fallback if a teammate's WSL lacks modules: one Ubuntu 24.04 VM (Multipass/VirtualBox) shared by the team.
Week 2 (1-7 Nov) Enforcement and deterministic classification. HTB root with four classes (realtime, streaming, besteffort, bulk), non-zero floors, ceil = link, fq_codel leaves, tc flower filters for protocol ip and ipv6, batched apply, readback verification, idempotent reset-to-safe; heuristic classifier (port/protocol/packet-size/pps, as qosify does) exposing confidence, with /correct; policy invariants unit-tested. Exit: Scenario 3 table E3 (Jain index across TVs, gamer p95 RTT, bulk floor never breached).
Week 3 (8-14 Nov) Capacity estimator. Load-gated AIMD with median-of-N probes against a slow EWMA baseline, refractory period, min/base/max clamps (cake-autorate pattern, attributed); unit-tested first against a simulated link model, then Scenario 2 (100 -> 20 Mbps at t=30 s) scored against ground truth: error %, convergence time, flips/min. Exit: E1 arm (ii) "open-loop AIMD" numbers. This is where WSL2 timing spikes (82 ms max on an idle 40 ms path [verified_fact]) bite; if flips are noisy, move headline runs to the VM or CI.
Week 4 (15-21 Nov) The differentiator: verify-or-rollback. Action ledger (trigger evidence, predicted KPI effect, window T, policy snapshot), post-window comparison, automatic restore and exponential backoff, watchdog returning to fq_codel-only on controller death or K consecutive rollbacks; fault-injection test E4 (bad policy at 150% of capacity; kill -9). Noise-injection variant of Scenario 2 (periodic 60 ms spikes, no capacity change). Exit: full three-arm E1 table (no controller / open-loop AIMD / verify-or-rollback) at N >= 10 with CIs, plus E4. If this week slips, drop Weeks 6's ML entirely.
Week 5 (22-28 Nov) Intent, dashboard, CPU, CI. FastAPI /intent {host|flow, class, ttl_s} validated against invariants, expiry, intent test inside Scenario 1; React or Chart.js dashboard reading /metrics and the evidence JSON (latency, jitter, loss, throughput, queue depth, fairness, ledger, classifier decisions with a correct button); CPU/RSS table E5; one GitHub Actions workflow that modprobes and fails fast, runs the suite, uploads artifacts (CAKE arm only if sch_cake loads on the runner, which is unconfirmed [unverified_assumption]); one IPv6 (ULA) run of Scenario 1.
Week 6 (29 Nov-5 Dec) Optional ML ablation and documentation. Early-flow GBM on NFStream features over self-generated labelled captures including an unseen-port UDP flow and a QUIC-like UDP/443 flow, reported against the heuristic baseline and shipped off by default if it does not win (E6); setup guide with exact versions and commands; THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md; known-limitations and emulation label; requirement -> module -> test -> evidence traceability table; the "implementation roadmap" the Unstop Round-2 text asks for [verified_fact, platform-level].
Week 7 (6-13 Dec) Freeze and package. 10-slide deck built only from report tables: (1) problem and scenarios, (2) six-component architecture, (3) module contracts (inputs/outputs/states/failure/success), (4) classifier accuracy, confidence, correction, (5) estimator vs ground truth, (6) verify-or-rollback ledger and fault injection, (7) latency/jitter/loss and fairness results, (8) three-arm adaptation/stability table with noise, (9) CPU, reproducibility (versions, seeds, CI link), dashboard, (10) limitations, production boundary, licences, roadmap. Annex: public repo, report.html, 2-3 minute recorded `make demo` hosted externally (keep the submitted file small; 5 MB precedent [unverified_assumption]); clean-clone rehearsal on a second machine; submit by 11 Dec.

Critical path: testbed + collector -> enforce -> estimator -> verify/rollback -> three-arm E1 table -> deck. Everything else (dashboard polish, ML, IPv6, CAKE, intent UI) can be cut without losing a criterion's evidence. Hard preconditions: root on every development machine; WSL >= 2.3.11 or a VM; iperf3/irtt installed; a public Git host for CI.
rubric_outcome_estimate:
The PDF lists five criteria and gives NO weights [source_derived_requirement]; they are treated as equal here. Prior independent estimates: specialist 7.8, blind judges 7.0 and 6.9, report target mean 7.2; the estimates below are what I think is realistically earned if the Week-4 differentiator lands, with the prior figures as the floor.

- "Accuracy of classification and link estimation": 6.5-7.0 (prior target 6.7, flagged hard). Link estimation is strong because error % and convergence time are scored against a capacity the script controls, something no autorate project publishes [verified_fact for the search]. Classification is the structural weakness: broad-category accuracy on self-generated captures is near-tautological [technical_inference] and QUIC/ECH limits any payload-free classifier; mitigations are held-out captures containing unseen-port and QUIC-like flows, a confidence histogram, and a demonstrated /correct path. Do not expect above 7 here.
- "Reduction in interactive latency, jitter and packet loss": 8.0-9.0 (prior target 8.0). The effect is already measured at 93.5% mean-RTT reduction on this machine [verified_fact, single run]; with N >= 10, p95/p99, IPDV and loss from irtt and bootstrap CIs this is the safest criterion in any of the five cases.
- "Fairness and absence of starvation": 7.5-8.0 (prior 7.3). HTB floors give a measurable guarantee; Jain index across the three TV streams and a "bulk floor never breached, including under an active intent" check are direct iperf3-JSON measurements.
- "Adaptation speed and policy stability": 6.5-7.5 (prior 6.7, flagged hard). Downside: WSL2 idle spikes can false-trigger an AIMD backoff and inflate flips [verified_fact for the spikes; technical_inference for the impact]. Upside: the three-arm table with injected noise is precisely the experiment that shows verify-or-rollback beating open-loop AIMD, which turns the hardest criterion into the most memorable slide. Outcome depends on Week 3-4 execution more than any other.
- "CPU overhead, reproducibility and clarity of results": 7.5-8.5 (prior 7.5). In-kernel enforcement, a ~1 Hz user-space loop measured with psutil, one-command seeded suite, exact versions, CI artefacts, report generator. The risk is documentation quality under time pressure, not feasibility.

Unweighted mean: 7.2-8.0 if executed, 6.9-7.2 if the estimator/rollback work is only partially delivered. Honest comparison: the prior model's Case 1 targets are ~8.0 (Round 1) and ~7.8 (Round 2), so on raw rubric expectation Case 1 is still ahead by roughly half a point; my case rests on shortlisting odds and field size under the one-slide format, not on a higher rubric mean. A platform-level overlay (HireToday lists "Innovation, Problem understanding, Solution quality, Implementation feasibility, Impact, Presentation quality") exists only as an unverified third-party listing [unverified_assumption]; if real, Case 3 scores well on Innovation and Impact and must not be assumed to outweigh the PDF criteria.
honest_weaknesses:
1. Skill fit is real, not imaginary: nobody on the team has demonstrated tc/HTB/namespace work; tc failures are silent (mis-steered flows fall into the default class with no error), shaping the wrong direction produces convincing but wrong numbers, and HTB quantum/r2q warnings already appeared in the smoke test [verified_fact]. AI assistance shortens the learning curve but cannot see kernel state; budget debugging time.
2. Environment fragility: everything needs root; only one laptop's WSL (2.6.1, kernel 6.6.87.2) has been checked and teammates' versions are unknown; sch_cake and sch_pie are absent, so the production-realistic reference needs a VM or CI; iperf3, irtt, nft are not installed yet; CAKE on the exact GitHub runner kernel (6.17.0-1022-azure) is unconfirmed [verified_fact for all].
3. WSL2 timing noise (82 ms max, 12.6 ms mdev on an idle 40 ms path) can false-trigger the estimator and inflate rate flips, threatening the stability criterion for reasons unrelated to the algorithm; headline runs may have to move to a VM or CI, costing tuning time not budgeted [verified_fact for the measurement; technical_inference for impact].
4. The classification criterion is structurally weak for everyone in 2026 (QUIC, ECH, DoH) and near-tautological on self-generated traffic; expect at most 7/10 on one fifth of the marks.
5. Domain-expert judges from Tata Elxsi's MCV vertical will know OpenWrt SQM, CAKE and cake-autorate; the latency win itself is delivered by fq_codel plus a correctly set shaper, not by the team's code, and if verify-or-rollback is not executed cleanly the project reads as a configuration exercise [technical_inference].
6. The PDF has no weights, no rounds and nine expected outputs; the single slide is harder to make convincing than Case 1's prescribed deck items, and the specialist never planned a Round-1 artefact (skeptic finding). The slide stands or falls on the evidence box.
7. The quantitative model disagrees with me: Case 1 ranked first under all four weighting schemes and all four input views, with both blind judges and all three adversarial reviewers; risk-adjusted 7.86 vs 7.26 and official-score potential 7.90 vs 7.23. My argument depends on hypotheses about assessor behaviour and field size [HYP] that no data on actual TELIPORT entrants supports.
8. The headline 638 -> 41 ms number is a single run with ping, not irtt, and must be re-run N >= 10 before it is cited anywhere; the "WSL2 emulation" label will invite "this is not a DOCSIS/GPON/Wi-Fi link" from a broadband judge, and the only honest answer is a relative comparison on identical topology.
9. Effort: seven modules plus docs plus deck in seven weeks for 2-3 students; the prior skeptic judged the specialist's estimates ~40% light; dashboard polish and ML are the classic scope sinks.
10. Prototype-as-annex compresses experiment evidence less well than Case 1's per-subset metrics table unless the report tables are designed for slides from Week 1; a 5 MB limit, if it holds for Season 4 [unverified_assumption], means the recording must be hosted externally.
11. Submitted ideas become Tata Elxsi's exclusive property [verified_fact, platform-level]; this applies equally to all cases but matters more for a project the team might want to publish later.

why_this_beats_the_other:
Under the now-known format (one slide to get shortlisted; a 10-slide deck with the prototype as an annex; a finale presentation to senior leaders), the comparison shifts from "which rubric is safer" to "which entry gets noticed, then survives a deck-only read, then lands with executives", and Case 3 wins each of those three steps for THIS team:

Round 1 (shortlisting). Case 1's slide can only contain design: an architecture line the PDF itself dictates, a cleaning approach, a model choice and triage rules; every competent team draws the same slide, and the one number it could add (RMSE 14.2) is the number every FD001 notebook gets [verified_fact for the baseline; HYP for the crowd]. Case 3's slide carries a 15x latency reduction from a reproducible script on the team's own machine, labelled as emulation, with the prior art named and the gap stated. The prior report concedes that "a 638 ms -> 41 ms latency plot is more memorable than a 14.2 RMSE on a benchmark with 53 public repos" and that Case 1 is "the most crowded and most templated of the five problems". With a provided dataset and explicit weights, Case 1 is also the likeliest to draw the largest pool, so shortlisting within it is the hardest [HYP]. Shortlisting is a prerequisite for every other mark; a slightly higher Round-2 ceiling is worth nothing if the slide is not read twice.

Round 2 (deck plus annex). Case 3's PDF prescribes exactly a prototype-as-annex evidence format: automated baseline-vs-optimised experiments, a scripted reset/impair/collect/report demonstration, a setup guide and a known-limitations section [source_derived_requirement]. The deliverable is the report and the repo, which is what the format accepts. Case 1's 40% on "Working pipeline" and "Demo & explanation" is, in a deck-only round, judged from screenshots of MLflow and Streamlit, and the red-team noted that this penalises exactly the interactive evidence the prior blueprint relies on. Case 3's weakest criterion (classification) is one fifth of unweighted marks; Case 1's weakest (Model performance, Dataset coverage) are weighted and flagged hard by both blind judges.

Finale (senior leaders, MCV vertical). The Case 3 story is one sentence an executive already believes, in Tata Elxsi's own communications domain, with a live or recorded before/after that anyone can read off a chart; the verify-or-rollback idea ("every change is a hypothesis; if it did not help, it is undone") is a product principle, not an ML detail. Case 1's edge (conformal lower-bound triage, leakage-audited decision replay) is real but is engineering hygiene that must be explained to be appreciated, which the prior report itself names as its single biggest risk.

Team fit under AI assistance. The modules that differentiate Case 3 (ledger, verification windows, invariants, intent API, experiment runner, CI, dashboard) are the team's stated strengths; the part they lack (tc semantics) is documented in man pages, has already been scripted successfully on this laptop, and is the kind of well-trodden, error-message-rich territory where an AI pair-programmer closes the gap fastest. In Case 1 every competitor has the same AI help and the ML is commodity, so AI assistance narrows Case 3's deficit more than it widens Case 1's lead [technical_inference].

What I am not claiming: the prior quantitative model still favours Case 1 by ~0.6 risk-adjusted, every reviewer ranked it first for a team without Linux fluency, and my format-based arguments are hypotheses about assessors and field size that no TELIPORT data confirms. The honest framing is the prior report's own: with networking fluency and time it is a toss-up or better for Case 3. The team can buy that fluency cheaply and reversibly: run the existing script on every machine on 19-20 Oct and produce a 5-run Scenario-1 report; if it reproduces, Case 3 has a slide no design-only entry can match and seven weeks of backend-shaped work ahead; if it does not, submit Case 1 with nothing lost.
